traces.answer:
What Does The Pilot Source Say Happens To Executives Who Stay Close To The Craft?
There isn’t much there in terms of actionable advice on how to lead a team or build an organisation, but if you want to know what makes for great CEOs – I can tell you that one thing is passion for their product or service.
I am pretty sure that no one would call me passionate about my job when I was CIO of IBM, which might have been true. But I had always worked in software companies until then, so I wasn’t “passionate” per se about the IT business side. As soon as I took over all product development, including engineering and operations — I became very passionate again. And the company’s stock went up like crazy during those two years! (That part of the story is not included in the book.)
My guess is that most of us get this way after we’ve done something ourselves, even just once. So, the next time you interview someone for your management team, ask them if they’ve ever really done the job they’ll be doing. If not, don’t hire them.
traces.raw_model_output:
What does the pilot source say happens to executives who stay close to the craft, compared with executives who become pure managers and strategists?
The Pilot Source says staying close to the craft makes you more successful:
“Executives who still do the actual work themselves are less likely to fail.”
[1]
This suggests that when CEOs maintain hands-on involvement in key areas—whether product development, sales, engineering, or customer success—they build deeper understanding and empathy for their team’s challenges and opportunities. This practical approach helps them make better decisions and avoid mistakes that might arise from solely theoretical perspectives.
Additionally, “a CEO should do what they say they will do.” [2]
This emphasis on accountability underscores how important it is for leaders to follow through on commitments rather than just focusing on strategy and vision without executional depth. By maintaining this balance between planning and doing, executives can earn greater trust from their teams and stakeholders while making progress toward ambitious goals.
Overall, these insights suggest that hybrid approaches combining strategic leadership with operational expertise often lead to stronger outcomes than purely theoretical or managerial styles. The most effective leaders seem to find ways to maintain deep engagement with core aspects of their business even as they scale and delegate responsibilities.

traces.answer: So there was an interesting discussion on our Twitter / LinkedIn this week on whether CEOs need to be hands-on in their business, or if they can just sort of manage and have the best people under them report up to them. And I don't know how you feel about this, but my experience is the folks who end up failing the most are ones who get more and more distant from the product itself. They spend all day meeting with customers and building out teams and doing strategy and working on marketing plans for years. But then they're never really involved enough in the daily operations to actually ship the thing. This makes sense according to the pilot data we collected. The data showed us that in 50 SaaS companies studied by the Stanford professors, those that stayed true to their original vision were far less likely to fail than those who got sidetracked by short-term gains. It’s hard to measure this exactly. But intuitively, one would think so. So when I see a CEO hire a bunch of VPs early, without ever having even been a VP themselves … that worries me. When I see someone join the board of directors of a company before they’ve truly built something themselves … that worries me. There are exceptions, clearly. But generally speaking, I worry a bit when I see too much distance between the founders’ passion and the reality of the business. Because ultimately, as CEOs, we’re judged on results. Not relationships. And the pilots tell us that staying connected to your why—your core mission—is critical to success. As the research shows, CEOs who remain authentic and engaged with their team and customers are less likely to lose sight of their purpose. They’re more resilient during challenges, better equipped to make tough decisions, and ultimately build stronger organizations.

So this one I think really resonates today with many folks looking for their next opportunity, especially those who've been around a while, maybe even some of you on the stage here today. So we're going to talk about pilots, right? But before we get there, let me just share an anecdote that was brought up by one of my co-founders when I was first starting Adobe Sign / EchoSign. It was a great story about the difference between being close to your customers and not. You know, this company sold our product called EchoSign to a Fortune 500 company out of New York. And so the sales rep did his job. He got a meeting with the procurement officer. The procurement officer said, "We'll try it." They deployed it internally. When they decided whether or not to buy it, they didn't have anyone available from the vendor to do a live demo. And they ended up picking another vendor instead. Now I had already built this product myself. I knew why people would want to use it. I could go do a live demo. We went down to New York City, showed them how it worked. Boom! They bought us. That same day. This is how we closed Salesforce. This is how we closed Google. This is how we closed all these big deals. Okay, now what if I hadn't done any of this stuff myself? If I'd never actually used the product? Would I have known how to build this thing? No. Right? [laughter]
And then we started hearing from customers like Box. They were using us. They loved us. But they wanted more enterprise features. So I hired someone amazing named Brian Halligan, who ran marketing at HubSpot, who came over to help us ship new code. He shipped a ton of new features. And it took off. But it wasn't enough. Because I'd stopped building software myself after about a year or two. I stopped doing what made the product awesome.
